first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent it, so I sat down with the iPad and read it properly. 'A Mexican wedding belongs to the whole family' is a nice way to open, and I was glad to see the Smartraveller warning right up in the key takeaways rather than buried. I read to the end. The middle has a lot of Spanish words and a lot of 'the study records', which slowed me down, but the paragraphs are short.

journey.quote: As at November 2026, Smartraveller advises Australians to "Exercise a high degree of caution" in Mexico overall, with higher levels for some states.
journey.reaction: Thank you for being straight with me. That's the first thing my husband would have looked up. It also means I'm now reading the rest of this rather nervously.

journey.section: What makes a traditional Mexican wedding: customs across Mexico
journey.quote: Ask both families early which customs matter most to them.
journey.reaction: Sensible. I'd want to ring the other mother before anyone books anything.

journey.section: 1. Before the wedding: la pedida de mano and the serenata
journey.quote: A study of weddings in Almoloya del Río, in the State of Mexico, describes three moments of the pedimento de mano, the aviso, the acuerdo and the contento, which have changed in their details but not in essence for at least two centuries.
journey.reaction: Interesting, but this reads like a university paper. By the third mention of Almoloya del Río I was skimming to find the part that tells me what we actually have to do.

journey.section: Who pays for a Mexican wedding
journey.quote: In many families the couple and their parents carry the main costs, and sponsors take on the item tied to their role as a gift. Hold that conversation early, and never assume what someone will offer.
journey.reaction: This is the paragraph I'm marking for my husband. Good to know the padrinos might cover the lazo or the cake, and good advice not to assume.

journey.section: 5. Mexican Catholic wedding traditions: the Mass and the kneeling cushions
journey.quote: Your parish priest will guide the order of service. Give each sponsor their cue and seat in writing.
journey.reaction: Practical and clear. In writing, yes. I like that.

journey.section: 6. The civil ceremony that makes it legal
journey.quote: A Mexican foreign ministry consulate page states that a religious marriage in Mexico does not replace the civil marriage, so a religious ceremony, if held, can follow the civil one.
journey.reaction: I didn't know that, and it matters. Two ceremonies means two days of getting elderly relatives dressed and transported, and probably paperwork in Spanish. Who handles that?

journey.section: 7. The callejoneada: a street parade to the party
journey.quote: The custom is closely associated with Guanajuato and Zacatecas, where the state government has described a callejoneada as an icebreaker before the wedding ceremony, with guests touring the historic centre.
journey.reaction: It sounds lovely, then further down I read that Guanajuato and Zacatecas are both on the 'Reconsider your need to travel' list. That rather spoiled it. And a walk over cobblestones is no good for my mother on her frame.

journey.section: 10. La víbora de la mar: the snake dance
journey.quote: Have two steady guests beside each chair.
journey.reaction: Ha, good. That's exactly the sort of thing I'd worry about.

journey.section: 13. Mexican weddings for Australians: marrying in Mexico or at home
journey.quote: It advises Australians to "Reconsider your need to travel" to Chiapas, Chihuahua, Colima, Guanajuato, Guerrero, Michoacán, north-western Durango, Sinaloa, Sonora, Tamaulipas and Zacatecas, each with listed exceptions.
journey.reaction: That's a long list. Honest, and dated, which I appreciate. But it tells me where not to go without telling me what anyone does to keep our family safe where we do go.

journey.quote: The hurricane and rainy season runs from June to November, and tropical storms and hurricanes can happen in other months.
journey.reaction: So what happens to our deposits if a hurricane cancels it? That's the question I'd ring about. 'A covered plan B' is fine for rain, not for a cancelled flight.

journey.quote: Couples who marry in Mexico tend to choose places outside the higher-level states: Mexico City, Oaxaca, the Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Baja California Sur, Jalisco and Nayarit among them.
journey.reaction: Helpful to have a short list. Nothing about flight times, transfers from the airport, or whether older or less mobile guests can manage, and nothing on medical care or travel insurance. That's my biggest worry and it isn't touched.

journey.quote: Before you book, put these questions to the Registro Civil where you will marry and to the Australian Embassy:
journey.reaction: Very useful. I'd print this list. It doesn't pretend to know the answers, which I trust more.

journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor is your single point of contact for venue, travel, vendors and guest rooms, works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, with the fee and inclusions confirmed in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: That's the sentence I was looking for. One person, Australian dollars, the fee in writing. It doesn't say who looks after us on the ground in Mexico or whether the supplier contracts are in English.

journey.quote: You deal with the registry, the Embassy and your parish directly.
journey.reaction: Fair enough to be clear about it, but that's the Spanish paperwork I was hoping someone would help with. I'd want to ask whether you at least point us to a translator.

unanswered_questions: If we pay deposits to venues or suppliers in Mexico, is that money protected, and what happens if a hurricane or a change in Smartraveller advice forces us to postpone?
Are contracts with Mexican suppliers in English, and are all quotes in Australian dollars?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong at 2am Mexico time? Is anyone from your side on the ground?
How would elderly or less mobile guests cope with the flights, airport transfers, cobbled streets and two separate ceremonies?
What travel insurance and medical cover should older guests have for Mexico?
Can you help find a certified Spanish translator for the registry documents, even if we deal with the registry ourselves?
Who is the Wedded Advisor, and can I speak to them on the phone before anything is booked?
would_share_with: My husband, with the who-pays paragraph, the Smartraveller list and the registry questions marked
My daughter, to ask whether a wedding at home with the Mass and mariachi might be simpler for Nana

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready to talk through dates, regions or a wedding at home, a Wedded Advisor is happy to start the conversation.
cta_reaction.why: 'A wedding at home' being offered as an option reassured me, and the fee in writing and AUD quotes help. I'd click if I knew it meant a phone call with a real, named person, and some idea of how deposits and safety are handled over there.

top_3_changes: In the Mexico section, add a short paragraph for older or less mobile guests: flights, airport transfers, cobbled streets, two ceremony days, travel insurance and medical cover, written as questions to ask rather than invented details.

Next to the hurricane line or the Wedded Advisor line, say plainly what happens after you click (a phone call with a named person) and how postponements, deposits and English-language contracts are handled, or list them as questions to ask.

Where the callejoneada is tied to Guanajuato and Zacatecas, note there and then that both are on the higher Smartraveller list, and cut back the repeated Almoloya del Río study detail so the practical tips stand out sooner.

The callejoneada section ties the custom to Guanajuato and Zacatecas, both on Smartraveller's 'Reconsider your need to travel' list. Worth a one-line cross-reference in that section?
